title: Treasury, IRS Announce Opportunity Zones Designations for Over 6,500 Communities Across America
body: November 5, 2026 The Working Families Tax Cuts Created a Permanent Process for States to Direct More Capital to Overlooked Communities WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) today announced the Qualified Opportunity Zone (QOZ) designations for all 50 states, territories, and the District of Columbia. Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the Opportunity Zone tax incentive was permanently renewed, enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities were added, and a process was established for redesignating zones every ten years. The new QOZ designations will become effective on January 1, 2027, and retain this designation for ten years. “Under President Trump’s leadership, the Working Families Tax Cuts permanently renewed and strengthened Opportunity Zones, giving investors, entrepreneurs, and local leaders the long-term certainty they need to commit capital to communities that have been overlooked for too long,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent . “Today’s announcement of the new designations will help direct private investment to these communities, expand economic opportunity, support job creation, and unlock long-term growth in these communities across the country.” “Thanks to the leadership of President Trump, Qualified Opportunity Zones were permanently extended and expanded by the Working Families Tax Cuts giving states an opportunity to attract long-term investment into underserved, rural, and economically distressed areas,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano . “By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most.” Background Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the permanent renewal of the Opportunity Zone tax incentives, including enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities, will continue to drive private investment in some of America’s most distressed communities. This builds on more than $110 billion in private-sector investment made since these tax incentives were established by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. The full list and map of designated Opportunity Zones are available here . On April 6, Treasury and the IRS released a list of 25,332 eligible census tracts across the country for nomination, of which 8,334 are in rural areas eligible for increased benefits as part of the Working Families Tax Cuts. On July 1, Treasury and the IRS began accepting nominations from Governors and the Mayor of the District of Columbia for eligible census tracts. An additional 130 eligible census tracts, of which 28 were in rural areas, were nominated during the statutory window. In total, 6,576 eligible census tracts were nominated by the end of the statutory window, of which 2,594 are in rural areas. All of the 6,576 eligible census tracts have been designated as QOZs effective January 1, 2027. Designation as a QOZ can help these 6,576 communities across the country attract new investment, create jobs, stimulate economic growth, and provide meaningful opportunities for residents. Additional information on nomination procedures was sent directly to the Governors and Mayor of the District of Columbia. The list of eligible census tracts is available here . The poverty rate and median family income for each tract can be found here . ###

title: November 5, 2026 - FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to a New Treatment for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
body: FDA News Release FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to a New Treatment for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma For Immediate Release: November 05, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval to Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. HNSCC is an aggressive, life-threatening disease for which there is a high unmet need for effective therapies. Rybrevant Faspro is not indicated as a treatment for patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma that is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Approval was based on trial results showing that more than double the percentage of patients responded to the drug compared to currently approved therapies. This is the first approval in 10 years of a drug for patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC who had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. “Today’s approval represents a meaningful step forward for patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a disease where treatment options have historically been limited and outcomes remain poor,” said Angelo De Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “This therapy offers patients and their physicians a new option with the potential to make a real difference in people’s lives.” The Accelerated Approval Program allows for earlier approval of drugs that treat serious conditions and fill an unmet medical need based on surrogate or intermediate endpoints. In this case, accelerated approval of Rybrevant Faspro was granted based on overall response rate and duration of response. Since it is not yet confirmed whether this will translate into a clinically meaningful benefit in long-term outcomes, the FDA has required confirmatory studies to verify and describe clinical benefit. In an open-label, multicenter clinical trial involving 102 patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, Rybrevant Faspro had an overall response rate of 42%, meaning these patients saw their tumor either decrease in size or disappear. Of those patients who had a response, 56% had a response lasting six months or longer. Currently approved therapies are associated with an overall response rate of around 20% or less and poor outcomes. The prescribing information for use as a single agent includes warnings and precautions for hypersensitivity and administration-related reactions, interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, dermatologic adverse reactions, ocular toxicity, and harm to an unborn baby. The FDA granted Rybrevant Faspro Breakthrough Therapy designation for this indication. The approval was granted to Janssen Biotech, Inc. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Global Maritime Fraud Network Supporting Iranian Regime
body: November 4, 2026 Network Circumvented Maritime Law to Enable Iran’s Shadow Fleet WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury targeted the vast criminal network of India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid , who have supported Iran’s shadow fleet through a web maritime fraud. Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies. “As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air.” False flags and fake maritime certifications allow vessels engaging in illicit activity to evade international regulations aimed at ensuring crew safety and safeguarding against environmental harm.  Falsely flagged vessels carry no valid protection and indemnity insurance, meaning that Iranian shadow fleet vessels operating under false flags could potentially cause billions of dollars in damages to the economies of the countries in whose territorial waters they operate. OFAC today also sanctioned Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc for its ongoing services in support of Iran’s aviation sector. Treasury has repeatedly warned that it will take action against those who continue to support Iran’s aviation industry, a key enabler of the regime’s destabilizing proliferation and terrorist activity. Concurrently with these designations, OFAC is issuing a new alert to industry to warn of the sanctions risks of dealing with potentially falsely flagged vessels, reemphasizing previous warnings from Treasury to the maritime industry to screen against unscrupulous actors such as Sharma and the vessels his network supports.  OFAC’s action also follows through on Treasury’s previous warning that any foreign firm or individual enabling sanctioned Iranian airlines—including through aircraft transfers, cargo services, or general sales agent support—will face serious consequences for supporting the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism.  The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026 and dubbed Economic D-Day , Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.  Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. Operation Economic Outcast also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . SHARMA CRIMINAL NETWORK For years, Suniel Kumar Sharma (Sharma) and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid (Shahid), have, through their base in Chandigarh, India, defrauded maritime regulatory administrations in multiple jurisdictions in order to establish false flagging authorities and maritime classification societies.  Purporting to represent nations from nearly every continent, from Guyana to Eswatini and Laos, Sharma and Shahid have allowed the Iranian shadow fleet, including those operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies, to evade international restrictions on their operation. Sharma and Shahid’s operations began as early as 2014, when the couple sought to impersonate the flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica.  In 2023, Sharma established the Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. (Eswatini Maritime), which, despite being publicly disavowed by Eswatini authorities, continues to provide flagging services for vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including the sanctioned vessel PING SHUN (IMO 9231901) , which at the time of its sanctioning had engaged in multiple shipments of Iranian oil. Many of Sharma and Shahid’s false flagging registries are not tied to registered companies, however.  In each case, the Sharma network purchases web domains, creating websites that claim to offer a variety of services on behalf of a country that has not authorized it to provide any of those services.  The services often include flagging, seafarer training and certification, and vessel classification, all of which are traditionally handled by legitimate organizations that hold vessels to strict international standards. Sharma’s network can be tied to multiple active websites that purport to belong to legitimate flagging registries.  Among these false representations are websites purporting to provide flagging services on behalf of Aruba, Guyana, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste, among others.  Sanctioned shadow fleet vessels have since gravitated towards these registries despite widespread awareness that they are not endorsed by the relevant governments.  For example, on April 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of War seized the false Guyana-flagged MAJESTIC X, formerly known as the PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was carrying Iranian oil at the time of its boarding. Sharma and Shahid additionally manage a network of primarily India-based entities, some of which are used to establish fraudulent flagging registries.  Sharma is the managing director of India-based Oceaniek Technologies India , a company he has used to establish duplicitous flag registries, including those purporting to belong to Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten.  Through these fraudulent registries Sharma has provided false flags to numerous sanctioned vessels that transport Iranian petroleum products, including LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570) , and VERA (IMO 9304655) . As Sharma’s activities have garnered greater attention, Shahid has stepped in to manage—at least on paper—the pair’s business empire, which includes companies ranging from financial services businesses to media streaming platforms.  Following press coverage of his activities, Sharma has closed down multiple deceitful registries, including the Laos Ship Registry and Maritime Safety Administration, previously known as the International Maritime Safety Agency of Guyana, a company that served as a false flagging agency for Guyana and was likely intended to similarly impersonate the Laotian government. In addition to Shahid, Indian nationals Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh nominally serve as directors of Sharma’s businesses, including India-based Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited . Suniel Kumar Sharma is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy.  Jaspreet Preeti Shahid is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Suniel Kumar Sharma. Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid. Oceaniek Technologies India is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Suniel Kumar Sharma. Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.  Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited. In addition, the following India-based companies are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid: Precept Trends Private Limited ; Polynesia Maritime Private Limited ; Alexarya Finserv Private Limited ; Alexarya Media and Entertainment Private Limited ; Viharaboating Private Limited ; and Aryavart Maritime and Educational Trust . GROUND HANDLING COMPANY SUPPORTING IRANIAN AIRLINES On August 24, 2026, Treasury issued determinations pursuant to E.O. 13902 against critical sectors––including aviation––that the Iranian regime uses to try to prop up its economy.  As Treasury has repeatedly highlighted, Iran uses its supposed “commercial” airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and its military, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and cash to its proxies.  Today, OFAC is taking action against a Türkiye-based ground handling company that continues to service sanctioned Iranian airlines, despite Treasury’s warnings of the sanctions risks associated with supporting Iran’s aviation sector. Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc provides ground handling and other services to several U.S.-designated Iranian airlines that continue to fly to Türkiye.  Fugo Ground Services Inc has direct service agreements with U.S.-sanctioned Iranian carriers including Iran Air Tour, Saha Airlines, Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Taban Airlines, and Ata Airlines Company, and began providing services to several of these carriers in the weeks after their September 8, 2026 designations . OFAC is designating Fugo Ground Services Inc pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.  Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior.  What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency.  In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.  OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities.  For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List. Click here for more information on the persons designated today. ###

title: Minutes of the Meeting of the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee November 3, 2026
body: November 4, 2026 The Committee convened in a closed session at the Department of the Treasury at 10:45 a.m.  All members were present.  Denise Rosenhaft Gray from BNY was also present to assist the Committee Chair.  Assistant Secretary for Financial Markets Hunter McMaster, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Federal Finance Brian Smith, Director of the Office of Debt Management Fred Pietrangeli, and Deputy Director of the Office of Debt Management Tom Katzenbach welcomed the Committee.  Other members of Treasury staff present were Abigail Brown, Chris Cameron, Dave Chung, Gabriella Csepe, Robert Dunsky, Chandler Elwyn, Gary Grippo, Salar Moghadam, Gavin Ross, Renee Tang, and Spencer Woodruff.  Federal Reserve Bank of New York staff members Ellen Correia Golay, Peggy Kauh, and Kyle Watson were also present. Director Pietrangeli highlighted changes in receipts and outlays through Q4 FY2026.  Within receipts, Pietrangeli cited a $159 billion (5%) increase in withheld and a $103 billion (9%) increase in non-withheld taxes.  These increases were offset by a $22 billion decrease in customs deposits, adjusting for tariff refunds, as well as a $43 billion (-9%) decrease in gross corporate taxes and a $27 billion increase (79%) in corporate refunds, the latter two attributed to provisions from the One Big Beautiful Bill.  In terms of outlays, Pietrangeli noted that the largest increases occurred at the Department of the Treasury, which rose by $122 billion (8%) due to higher gross interest resulting from higher levels of debt, and at the Department of Health and Human Services, which rose by $120 billion (6%) because of higher Medicare and Medicaid spending. Pietrangeli then turned to deficit and privately-held net marketable borrowing projections, noting that the median primary dealer’s aggregate FY2027-28 privately-held net marketable borrowing estimate was nearly unchanged since last quarter’s Committee meeting.  He noted that current issuance sizes would result in a modest funding shortfall in FY2027 relative to projected borrowing needs, but that the gap could likely be managed using bills.  However, looking ahead to FY2028-2029, the median primary dealer forecast for privately-held net marketable borrowing implies a $2.14 trillion funding shortfall based on current coupon auction sizes and privately-held bill supply. Debt Manager Dunsky next reviewed primary dealers’ feedback on whether Treasury should avoid scheduling Treasury bill and floating rate note (FRN) auctions on days when the Federal Open Market Committee is expected to release a statement (i.e., “FOMC days”), which would be consistent with its existing scheduling practices for nominal coupons and TIPS.  Almost all primary dealers favored no change to the auction schedule.  Primary dealers pointed to operational complexities associated with conducting more auctions on the surrounding days as generating a greater cost than any benefit associated with avoiding bill and FRN auctions on FOMC days. Overall, dealers do not currently see bill and FRN auctions on FOMC days as a problem. Debt Manager Elwyn then summarized primary dealers’ views on the effects of the larger liquidity-support buyback operations announced on August 19 for the 10- to 20-year and 20- to 30-year sectors, as well as potential enhancements to the buyback program. Most dealers reported at least modest improvements in liquidity and market functioning, citing a more dependable outlet for off-the-run securities, less risk of price dislocations, and more stable relative-value relationships, although the effect on dealers’ ability to intermediate client flows was mixed. Recommendations from primary dealers included clearer and earlier communication, broader distribution of purchases through per-CUSIP limits, and smaller, more frequent operations. Some dealers noted that concentrated purchases increased the risk of “missing” the buyback and having to manage the associated duration exposure. Dealers also discussed spread-based pricing and switch transactions, both of which have been discussed previously and would require further exploration and significant time and effort to implement. Deputy Director Katzenbach next recapped primary dealers’ thoughts on trends in structural demand for Treasuries.  Money market mutual funds, stablecoins, and the Federal Reserve System Open Market Account (SOMA) were identified as potential sources of growing demand for bills, while respondents pointed to increased bank demand in the belly of the curve.  Conversely, primary dealers had mixed views about market demand for longer-dated securities from liability-driven investors. Katzenbach then reviewed primary dealers’ expectations for coupon issuance.  Respondents generally expected Treasury to begin increasing nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes by the end of FY2027, and overwhelmingly expected Treasury to focus the eventual increases in short- and intermediate-dated tenors.  Katzenbach noted that several primary dealers reiterated their view that Treasury should consider issuing a 1-year SOFR-indexed FRN.  The Committee agreed that exploring potential issuance of SOFR-indexed FRNs would be worthwhile and suggested that multiple tenors be considered in light of potential interest from different investor types. The Committee adjourned at 11:50 a.m. for lunch. The Committee reconvened at 1:00 p.m. The Committee then discussed the first charge, which addressed the recent trends in corporate borrowing related to super intelligence (SI) and associated businesses.  The presenter stressed that borrowing in the SI sector is constantly evolving as new issues are announced nearly every week.  Additionally, the sector is expected to continue to ramp up borrowing in 2027 as the demand for computing capacity outstrips supply into 2028.  The presenter asserted that competition for capital currently appears to be contained within the tech credit ecosystem, and that there is no clear evidence that SI-related issuance is crowding out Treasuries or non-tech credit.  Lastly, the presenter attributed the rise seen in the 10-year Treasury yield primarily to capex-driven economic growth that has pushed real yields higher, with additional upward pressure from energy price shocks. The Committee next discussed the second charge, which evaluated the growth in the use of Treasury derivatives, in particular swaps and futures. The presenter noted that certain types of investors prefer to obtain leveraged duration exposure through derivatives for liquidity and operational reasons. Compared to buying cash Treasuries and obtaining leverage through repo markets, derivatives typically provide more favorable accounting treatment, have implicit financing costs that are not reported as explicit expenses, and reduce rollover risk for financing. Tax considerations were highlighted as another relevant factor for some investors. To increase the attractiveness of using cash Treasuries, the presenter suggested that policymakers could consider options to lessen balance sheet constraints of holding cash Treasuries, evaluate potential changes to expense, accounting and tax treatment, incentivize institutions to build repo infrastructure, reduce operational frictions associated with Treasury settlement, and minimize legal and regulatory challenges associated with onboarding as a repo transaction counterparty. The Committee adjourned at 2:45 p.m. The Committee reconvened at 3:00 p.m. The Chair summarized key elements of the Committee report for Secretary Bessent and followed with a discussion of recent market developments. Finally, the Committee turned to its financing recommendation for the current quarter and unanimously recommended that Treasury maintain nominal coupon, FRN, and TIPS auction sizes at current levels but also consider adjusting its forward guidance language.  The Committee agreed that in light of projected borrowing needs, increases in coupon auction sizes would likely be appropriate in the second half of FY2027. Members generally agreed that additional issuance should be concentrated in the 2- to 10-year sector, and had a meaningful discussion about potential future changes to 20-year and 30-year issuance. The Committee adjourned at 4:05 p.m. _________________________________ Brian Smith Deputy Assistant Secretary for Federal Finance United States Department of the Treasury November 3, 2026 Certified by: _________________________________ Jason Granet, Chair Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee November 3, 2026 Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee Quarterly Meeting Committee Charge – November 3, 2026 Fiscal Outlook Taking into consideration Treasury’s short, intermediate, and long-term financing requirements, as well as the variability in financing needs from quarter to quarter, what changes, if any, do you recommend to Treasury issuance?  Please also provide perspectives regarding market expectations for Treasury issuance, the effects of changes in SOMA holdings, the evolution of Treasury holdings by different types of investors, as well as auction calendar construction. SI-related Issuance Please summarize recent trends in corporate bond issuance related to super intelligence and associated businesses. How much of such issuance has occurred to date and is projected for the future. What types of investors are the primary buyers of such debt? To what extent does such debt issuance compete with Treasury securities for investor demand? What other potential effects on fixed income markets should Treasury be monitoring? Treasury Derivatives Please comment on the growth in the use of Treasury derivatives, in particular swaps and futures. How has use of these derivatives evolved? Who are the primary users and what factors have driven their usage? How do these derivatives affect demand for cash Treasury securities? What effects do these derivatives have on Treasury repo markets? Does the use of derivatives by investors reduce the size of the Treasury repo market? Should Treasury consider any policy initiatives to increase demand for cash Treasury securities relative to Treasury derivatives? Financing this Quarter We would like the Committee’s advice on the following: The composition of Treasury notes and bonds to refund approximately $97 billion of privately-held notes and bonds maturing on November 15, 2026. The composition of Treasury marketable financing for the remainder of this refunding quarter and the next refunding quarter.

title: Report to the Secretary of the Treasury from the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
body: November 4, 2026 Dear Mr. Secretary, Since the TBAC last met in early August, Treasury markets have repriced toward a higher path for interest rates, reflecting stronger economic activity and associated financing needs, persistent energy-supply disruptions, and the Federal Reserve’s initial rate hike and projections for further increases. The selloff in rates was led by the front end of the yield curve, with two-year yields rising by roughly 50bps and ten-year yields by roughly 40bps. The move accelerated in September and early October, with ten-year yields peaking around 5.4% and thirty-year yields around 5.7% in early October. Some of that increase has since reversed. A substantial part of the repricing reflected stronger U.S. economic activity through the summer despite higher energy prices and rising rates. Household spending remained resilient as gains in financial wealth and lower savings rates cushioned pressure on real incomes. Existing fixed-rate mortgages limited the increase in homeowners’ debt-service costs, even as higher rates on new borrowing weighed on housing activity. Meanwhile, strong investment in computing equipment, intellectual property, and data centers offset weakness in more rate-sensitive investment. The infrastructure buildout proved less sensitive to financing costs than traditional housing-led expansions. Related gains in construction and equipment manufacturing are becoming visible but have not yet generated a broad acceleration in employment. This resilience gave the Federal Reserve greater scope to respond to persistent inflation risks exacerbated by the energy shock. Supply disruptions that began over the summer have proved more persistent than initially expected, keeping crude and refined-product prices elevated through the quarter and feeding into transportation and freight costs. Headline CPI accelerated to 3.7% in September, with gasoline alone accounting for more than half of the monthly increase. Core CPI ran at 2.6% as fuel and freight costs passed through to other categories. The Federal Reserve responded in September by raising its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Chairman Warsh emphasized both the strengthening economy and insufficient progress on inflation, characterizing the decision as removing accommodation rather than making already restrictive financial conditions materially tighter. The September Summary of Economic Projections reinforced the higher-for-longer message: the median policy-rate projection rose to 4.1% for both year-end 2026 and year-end 2027, compared with 3.8% and 3.6%, respectively, in June. Markets continued to price approximately three additional rate increases over the coming year even as the Fed held rates steady in October. More recently, higher borrowing costs and emerging weakness in equity and credit markets have moderated expectations for the pace of tightening but not eliminated expectations for further increases. Several cross-market and technical developments came into play over the quarter: Term premium has risen less than yields this year, though the ten-year term premium showed some strain in the early fall. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s ACM model estimate of the ten-year term premium rose approximately 20bps in September. Interest rate implied volatility rose sharply, reflecting greater priced uncertainty and raising the cost of option-based protection against further yield increases. As yields rose and refinancing incentives diminished, mortgage durations extended, prompting convexity hedgers to reduce duration. Collateralized mortgage obligation floaters with coupon caps added to hedging pressures as forward-implied coupons approached their caps, likely increasing demand for intermediate-dated rates volatility. These flows likely amplified the initial selloff and increase in volatility, although the scope for further mortgage-duration extension diminished as yields moved higher. Stronger economic activity was also driving expectations of higher interest rates outside the United States. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan raised policy rates over the period as markets priced a broader tightening cycle across major developed economies. Developments in European sovereign markets were also relevant for Treasuries, as fiscal and political uncertainty produced a sharp widening in French government-bond spreads, adding to volatility across global fixed-income markets. Those linkages have not operated uniformly: the correlation between French and U.S. yield changes weakened in October, and more acute French stress subsequently supported safe-haven demand for Treasuries and German Bunds. Technology-related financing remained an additional influence on capital markets and financial conditions. Large debt offerings and prospective mega-IPOs reflected substantial private-sector financing needs. Heavy technology issuance and uncertainty over future financing needs contributed to wider spreads in the sector and increased competition for long-duration capital. Banks and asset managers also helped technology companies tap a broader pool of capital through GPU-backed loans, equipment leases, and data center project financing. Foreign investor demand to finance U.S. technology contributed to dollar strength, providing an additional channel of financial tightening alongside higher borrowing costs. Although large issuance windows may influence Treasury concessions and hedging flows at the margin, there is no evidence of a persistent deterioration in Treasury auction demand. Recent auctions remained generally resilient, though individual results varied. Technology news also contributed to weaker risk sentiment later in the period, helping restore demand for Treasuries. By late October, the Nasdaq 100 had fallen just over 7% from its early-October high amid greater scrutiny of the returns on increasingly debt-financed technology investment. Together with wider credit spreads, the equity pullback helped restore a safe-haven bid for Treasuries, partially reversing the earlier rise in yields. Against that backdrop, the Committee convened for its quarterly refunding discussion. The outlook shows the funding gap widens over FY27 and increases further in FY28 and FY29. Consistent with Treasury’s cash management policy, Treasury recently published cash balance assumptions for the end of Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 at approximately $850 billion and $1 trillion, respectively. The Committee next addressed the first of its two charges: Super Intelligence (SI)-related issuance. Members discussed recent trends in corporate bond issuance related to SI and associated businesses. Members noted the market is in the midst of a significant technology financing cycle. Financing is also expanding beyond long-dated corporate bonds, with secured and asset-backed structures increasingly bringing issuance inside 10 years. Taken as a whole, the technology ecosystem appears to have both the capacity and incentive to sustain borrowing and investment. Foreign demand for U.S. fixed-income assets has accelerated this year, while the broader investor base retains significant capacity to absorb additional issuance. Insurers, pensions, households, and foreign investors provide diversified sources of demand, with households and private pensions still relatively under allocated to fixed income. Even modest reallocations from cash and equities could therefore absorb a meaningful share of projected borrowing. Treasury auction results show no evidence that 2026 technology-related issuance has crowded out long-end Treasury demand. To the extent technology investment is affecting rates, the Committee viewed the transmission as stemming from stronger growth rather than through crowding out. Higher Treasury yields have primarily reflected growth, policy expectations, and energy prices rather than an issuance-driven supply shock. Members emphasized, however, that the financing cycle remains in its early stages and recommended that Treasury continue to monitor potential effects on Treasury market demand as SI-related issuance grows. The Committee’s second charge focused on Treasury derivatives and their growing role in the market. Since the 2022 rise in yields, asset managers have increasingly used futures to gain synthetic Treasury exposure, while liability-driven investors, including pension funds and insurers, have used interest rate swaps to manage duration. The Committee emphasized that expressing duration through derivatives enhances demand for Treasuries by broadening market access and expanding intermediation capacity. In the context of discussing derivatives, the Committee identified several policy options that could further improve demand for cash Treasuries. These include easing regulatory constraints on balance sheet capacity, including exempting Treasuries from leverage ratios and recognizing pre-positioned discount window collateral in liquidity metrics; expanding access to repo financing; improving the availability of term repo; and enabling new entrants in repo market making. The Committee also recommended evaluation of fund accounting treatment of repo interest, tax treatment, and operational challenges. Together, these steps could broaden and diversify the base of cash Treasury holders, strengthen market intermediation, and support durable demand for Treasuries. The Committee discussed the efficacy of the liquidity support buyback program. There is a variety of evidence that the program has supported liquidity conditions since it was introduced in 2024, and buybacks remain an effective tool for that purpose. While an effective tool, the Committee believes that any management of Treasury’s maturity profile should be done via changes to auction sizes. To further the goal of financing the government at the lowest cost over time, the Committee continues to endorse an issuance strategy that balances expected costs and volatility of interest expense, matches issuance patterns to market demand, encourages smooth market functioning, and is regular and predictable. As members look ahead, baseline fiscal projections suggest that current auction sizes are likely to shift Treasury’s debt profile toward an increasing share of bill and shorter-term funding. The Committee believes that the market has recently been absorbing Treasury issuance well and that the bulk of recent interest rate rises reflect strong economic conditions and the monetary policy outlook rather than weak investor demand for Treasuries. The Committee discussed that real money investors, including retail and some institutional investors, have grown their demand as rates have risen and as a hedge against downward moves in economic conditions. However, the Committee also noted that money market fund assets have leveled off and the bill market has started to show some signs of price sensitivity. In light of that outlook, for the current quarter, the Committee recommended keeping nominal coupon, FRN, and TIPS auction sizes unchanged. However, the Committee believes that given current fiscal projections, increases in coupon auction sizes will be warranted later in FY27. Looking ahead, given the projected funding gaps in FY28 and FY29, members discussed different approaches to coupon increases over the horizon. While there is broad agreement across the Committee to increase coupon auction sizes, there was considerable debate around the pace and sizing specific to the long end of the curve. Members recommended that Treasury change its forward-guidance language and emphasized that clear communication alongside a regular and predictable operating framework remains important to help market participants adjust to future changes. In conclusion, consistent with its past messaging, the Committee encourages Congress to act to raise or suspend the debt limit to avoid disrupting Treasury market functioning, increasing costs to the taxpayer, and constraining economic growth. Respectfully, Jason S. Granet Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee E. Alexander Schiller Vice Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee

title: Quarterly Refunding Statement of Assistant Secretary for Financial Markets Hunter McMaster
body: November 4, 2026 WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of the Treasury is offering $125 billion of Treasury securities to refund approximately $97 billion of privately-held Treasury notes and bonds maturing on November 15, 2026.  This issuance will raise new cash from private investors of approximately $28 billion.  The securities are: A 3-year note in the amount of $58 billion, maturing November 15, 2029; A 10-year note in the amount of $42 billion, maturing November 15, 2036; A 30-year bond in the amount of $25 billion, maturing November 15, 2056. The 3-year note will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Monday, November 9, 2026.  The 10-year note will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026.  The 30-year bond will be auctioned at 1:00 p.m. ET on Thursday, November 12, 2026.  All these auctions will take place on a yield basis and will settle on Monday, November 16, 2026. The balance of Treasury financing requirements over the quarter will be met with regular weekly bill auctions, cash management bills (CMBs), and monthly note, bond, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), and 2-year Floating Rate Note (FRN) auctions. NOMINAL COUPON AND FRN FINANCING Treasury believes its current auction sizes leave it well positioned to address potential changes to the fiscal outlook and to the size and composition of the SOMA portfolio.  Based on current projected borrowing needs, Treasury anticipates maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for the next several quarters.  Treasury is monitoring SOMA purchases of Treasury bills and growing demand for Treasury bills from the private sector.  Looking ahead, Treasury continues to evaluate potential future changes to nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes, with a focus on trends in structural demand and potential costs and risks of various issuance profiles.  As part of that process, Treasury will engage with a variety of market participants to better understand evolving Treasury supply and demand dynamics. In considering any changes, Treasury will be guided by the objective of financing the government at the lowest cost over time. The table below presents, in billions of dollars, the actual auction sizes for the August to October 2026 quarter and the anticipated auction sizes for the November 2026 to January 2027 quarter: 2-Year 3-Year 5-Year 7-Year 10-Year 20-Year 30-Year FRN Aug-26 69 58 70 44 42 16 25 28 Sep-26 69 58 70 44 39 13 22 28 Oct-26 69 58 70 44 39 13 22 30 Nov-26 69 58 70 44 42 16 25 28 Dec-26 69 58 70 44 39 13 22 28 Jan-27 69 58 70 44 39 13 22 30 Treasury plans to address any seasonal or unexpected variations in borrowing needs over the next quarter through changes in regular bill auction sizes and/or CMBs. TIPS FINANCING Over the November 2026 to January 2027 quarter, Treasury plans to maintain TIPS auction sizes at current levels: the November 10-year TIPS reopening auction size at $19 billion, the December 5-year TIPS reopening auction size at $24 billion, and the January 10-year TIPS new issue auction size at $21 billion. BILL ISSUANCE Treasury continues to see strong demand for bill securities from a broad range of market participants.  Based on current forecasts, Treasury expects to maintain current auction sizes of benchmark bills into late November and anticipates potentially issuing a short-dated CMB to meet its cash management needs around the end of November.  Given projections for receipts associated with the mid-December corporate and non-withheld tax date, Treasury expects to implement reductions to shorter-dated bill auction sizes during the month of December.  In January, Treasury anticipates increasing auction sizes across the bill curve based on expected seasonal fiscal outflows.  As always, Treasury will continue to evaluate near-term borrowing needs and assess additional adjustments to bill auction sizes as appropriate. CONVERSION OF 7-YEAR NOTE TO QUARTERLY NEW ISSUE Treasury plans to convert the 7-year note from a monthly new issue to a quarterly new issue with two reopenings (similar to the 10-year note).  The 7-year note will continue to be auctioned towards the end of each month and issue and mature at month end.  Treasury will auction new issues in March, June, September, and December and conduct reopening auctions in the subsequent two months of each cycle.  This conversion will go into effect beginning with the March 2027 new issue, which will be reopened in April and May. CASH BALANCE Treasury is assuming an $850 billion cash balance at the end of December.  However, based on current projections for the upcoming refunding quarter, Treasury estimates that the size of the Treasury General Account (TGA) could peak at $1.025 trillion (plus or minus $50 billion) in late November and late January.  These figures are consistent with Treasury’s long-standing cash balance policy and are driven by the large outflows expected to occur at those times. BUYBACKS Treasury is releasing a tentative buyback schedule for the upcoming refunding quarter.  Treasury anticipates that, over the course of the upcoming quarter, it will purchase up to $70 billion in off-the-run securities across buckets for liquidity support and up to $25 billion in the 1-month to 2-year maturity bucket for cash management purposes.  Treasury will continue to evaluate possible enhancements to buyback operations such as changes to maximum purchase amounts, buyback operation scheduling and frequency, security eligibility, and execution process. Please send comments or suggestions on these subjects or other subjects related to debt management to debt.management@treasury.gov . The next quarterly refunding announcement will take place on Wednesday, February 3, 2027. ###

title: November 2, 2026 - FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality
body: FDA News Release FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality FDA issues final guidance for cell and gene therapy manufacturers, recommends building potency assurance into every stage of a therapy’s lifecycle — from early development through patient delivery For Immediate Release: November 02, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically. The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement. "Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research . "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety." The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies. By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence. The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance. title: October 30, 2026 - FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms For Immediate Release: October 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options. “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) . “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.” The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit. RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11).  Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells. The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment. The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site. The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. October 22, 2026 - FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus to coordinate agency action on brain and nervous system conditions, with inaugural focus on Alzheimer's prevention For Immediate Release: October 22, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced the launch of the Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus (NAIN) , a new agency program aligned with the Trump Administration’s efforts to accelerate medical innovation and deliver breakthrough treatments. NAIN is designed to advance the science, tools, and regulatory approaches needed to support the development of medical products for conditions affecting the brain and nervous system. NAIN’s inaugural initiative, the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator , will focus on advancing medical products that help delay or prevent Alzheimer's disease. Both efforts support the National Alzheimer’s Project Act (NAPA), the federal government's comprehensive roadmap for coordinated action on Alzheimer's and related dementias. "The launch of NAIN reflects FDA's commitment — in support of the Trump Administration’s drive to transform health care innovation — to making sure our regulatory science and cross-center collaboration keep pace with the rapid advances happening in neuroscience," said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. "Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, we are bringing the full breadth of FDA's expertise to bear on one of the most urgent public health challenges of our time.” Developing medical products for neuroscience indications is associated with complex scientific and clinical challenges, including limited understanding of underlying biology, variable disease presentation, and difficulties in demonstrating meaningful clinical benefit, particularly for conditions that develop over many years. Advances in biomarkers, digital health technologies, and other medical product development tools, however, offer important opportunities to address these challenges. NAIN will bring together scientific and regulatory expertise from the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and Center for Devices and Radiological Health to address scientific and regulatory questions that benefit from coordinated consideration across drugs, biologics, and devices. NAIN will encompass conditions that affect the brain and nervous system broadly, including neurologic and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and pain. NAIN will also support robust engagement with patients, industry, academia and other stakeholders to advance these efforts. As its first initiative, NAIN is launching the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator . This inaugural initiative will draw on perspectives from across the FDA and engage patients and caregivers, researchers, industry, public-private partnerships and other government agencies. The initiative will explore innovative approaches to advancing clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease prevention and early-intervention drug development with emphasis on trial populations, stage-appropriate endpoints, and evidentiary approaches for demonstrating prevention or delay of cognitive decline due to Alzheimer’s disease. The FDA has long been committed to supporting the development of safe and effective medical products that address diseases and conditions of the brain and nervous system. Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, the agency is taking a proactive, coordinated approach to accelerating progress, bringing together its scientific and regulatory expertise, engaging the broader research and development community, and working in concert with federal partners to meet the scale of this public health challenge. title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software
body: FDA News Release FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software New policy clarifies when app content requires FDA review and how drug-connected software must be described on medication labels For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency. “Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.” The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users. The guidance identifies two categories of companion software: Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used. Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising. “This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.” “Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology . “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.” This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on. The final guidance is available here . title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration yesterday approved the first generic of Climara Pro (estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system, 0.045 mg per day/0.015 mg), a transdermal hormone therapy patch for women with an intact uterus applied once a week. The approval aligns with FDA’s Public Health Pillar : Increasing Access to Affordable Medicines & Medical Products. “Menopause is a universal experience for women, and it can greatly affect a person’s quality of life. This approval makes effective treatment more accessible,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Approvals like this reflect FDA’s ongoing commitment to expanding American patient access to safe, affordable, high-quality medications.” The generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system is therapeutically equivalent to Climara Pro, which is indicated for use in women with an intact uterus for: Treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause Prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system contain both estrogen and progestogen in a single patch; this differs from estrogen-only patches commonly used in menopause treatment. Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are specifically approved for women with an intact uterus, as the progestogen component is included to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with estrogen use alone. “Once-weekly dosing can make a real difference in how patients manage their care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “A patch offers a convenient alternative to daily oral medications, which may help patients stay on track with their treatment.” Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are contraindicated in patients with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; breast cancer or a history of breast cancer; estrogen-dependent neoplasia; active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE) or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease or a history of these conditions; known anaphylactic reaction or angioedema or hypersensitivity to estradiol and levonorgestrel; hepatic impairment or disease; and protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders. The most common adverse reactions (greater than or equal to 5%) are: application site reaction, vaginal bleeding, breast pain, upper respiratory infection, back pain, depression, pain, headache and flu syndrome. In the U.S., nine out of 10 prescriptions filled are for generic drugs. Increasing the availability of generic drugs helps to create competition in the marketplace, which then helps to make treatment more affordable and increases access to healthcare for more patients. Learn more about the FDA Drug Competition Action Plan . Climara Pro is a registered trademark of Bayer. The FDA approved Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA) Inc.’s Estradiol and Levonorgestrel Transdermal System. Please contact the manufacturer for information about the medicine’s availability. title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment New treatment may allow some patients to maintain viral control after stopping all hepatitis B therapy For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements. Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review . The approval was granted to GSK plc. October 19, 2026 - FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery For Immediate Release: October 19, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life. Patients with locally advanced rectal cancer often receive chemotherapy and radiation prior to surgery, which can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility. Surgery also carries risks of serious, sometimes life-threatening complications, including poor healing and leaks where the bowel is reconnected, and in some patients, permanent colostomy. “The FDA is committed to closing the gap between scientific progress and patient access, and that commitment has to show up not just in policy, but in the pace of our work,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “American patients deserve timely access to innovative treatments, and the Trump Administration is making that a reality. Completing this review nearly 4 months ahead of schedule means some patients who might otherwise be preparing for surgery, radiation or chemotherapy may now have a different conversation with their doctor.” Today’s approval is for Jemperli used alone in adults with previously untreated stage II or stage III locally advanced rectal cancer. At these stages, the cancer has grown into nearby tissue or reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. To be eligible, patients’ tumors must be mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), as determined by an FDA-authorized test. Published estimates suggest that approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR or MSI-H. Both terms describe a defect in the way cancer cells correct errors when copying their DNA. Normally, a built-in repair system catches and fixes these mistakes. When the system does not work properly, errors accumulate and create proteins the immune system can recognize, making these tumors particularly vulnerable to immunotherapy. Jemperli works by blocking a signal that cancer cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. Specifically, it targets a protein called PD-1 on immune cells. “Standard treatment for rectal cancer has major life-changing effects. For certain types of rectal cancer, this approval represents a groundbreaking option that avoids surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. This represents a significant benefit for patients and their families,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “The FDA is acting on emerging evidence to bring new approaches to patients sooner, while requiring further studies to confirm that these treatments provide lasting benefits.” The FDA based its decision on interim results from AZUR-1 ( NCT05723562 ), a phase 2 study evaluating Jemperli alone in 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. In the study, patients received up to nine doses of Jemperli, given every 3 weeks over 6 months. After a median follow-up of more than 2 years — meaning at least half of patients had been monitored for that long — almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Longer follow-up is needed to understand the duration of response and how often the cancer returns. An earlier study at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center ( NCT04165772 ) evaluated Jemperli alone in 50 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. None of the patients had detectable signs of cancer after Jemperli treatment, and nearly all patients (93%) maintained that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. Of the 27 patients followed for at least 3 years, only one had their cancer return, and it recurred in the same area. Jemperli can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs and tissues. These reactions can be severe or fatal. The most common side effects, reported in at least 15% of patients treated for this type of rectal cancer, were fatigue, rash, diarrhea and itching. The FDA granted Priority Review to the application and Breakthrough Therapy designation to Jemperli for the treatment of dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. This action marks the 11th approval of a drug reviewed under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program , which aims to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities. Because this is an accelerated approval based on interim trial results, the sponsor must continue following patients to show these responses create lasting clinical benefit. The approval was granted to GSK.
